Journal.Title: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics

Article.ArticleTitle: Prototype-Guided Multi-Task Learning for HCC Postoperative Complications Prediction.

Abstract.AbstractText: Postoperative complications following hepatectomy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remain frequent and are associated with increased mortality and healthcare costs. Existing predictive models often struggle with extreme class imbalance and fail to capture the holistic complication burden by treating risks as disjointed tasks. To overcome these limitations, we propose PMCP, a novel Prototype-Guided Multi-task Complication Prediction framework designed to jointly predict the holistic Comprehensive Complication Index (CCI) alongside four specific severe complications within 24 hours postoperatively. PMCP leverages a large language model to distill unstructured clinical narratives, orchestrating an adaptive fusion with longitudinal structured electronic health records to circumvent modality laziness. To counteract majority class suppression, we introduce a dual-prototype mechanism that selectively amplifies rare, high-risk clinical signals and maintains distinct feature space separation. Evaluated on the real-world clinical cohort, our framework significantly outperformed state-of-the-art baselines. PMCP achieved an AUC of 0.800 for CCI, and AUCs of 0.935, 0.798, 0.798, and 0.887 for the four specific complications, respectively. Furthermore, the model exhibited a strong capacity to maintain predictive performance even with 40% missing structured data. In summary, PMCP provides a promising framework for early postoperative complication risk assessment and may support individualized monitoring and intervention planning after hepatectomy.

Article.ArticleTitle: New Large Language Models Outperform Older Models and Hallucinate Less in Operative Note Data Extraction.

Abstract.AbstractText: Recent improvements in large language models (LLMs) may provide a scalable solution for registry data curation. However, trust in model outputs remains limited by hallucinations, wherein models invent information. Given the rapid pace of LLM development, the purpose of this study was to compare the accuracy and hallucination rates of a "newer" and an "older" and previously evaluated LLM in extracting total hip arthroplasty (THA) operative variables.

Surgical approach, fixation technique, and bearing surface were manually abstracted from 1,000 primary THA operative notes from 47 different surgeons. Using 25% of the dataset, we iteratively developed prompts to query two locally hosted LLMs (one released in 2024, the older model, and the other released in 2026, the newer model) to extract those three data points. We tested the extraction pipeline for the best prompts on the remaining 75% of the dataset. We calculated performance metrics and manually assessed 100 sample output reasonings from each model for hallucinations.

Overall Performance: The newer model exhibited higher accuracy than the older model across all three data extraction tasks: surgical approach (98 versus 96%), fixation technique (98 versus 96%), and bearing surface (93 versus 89%). For each task, the highest-performing prompt technique for the newer model was comparatively simpler than the highest-performing prompt technique for the older model. Hallucination Rate Analyses: Across all evaluated extraction domains, the newer model demonstrated significantly lower hallucination rates compared with the older model. Hallucination rates for surgical approach, fixation technique, and bearing surface extraction were 5, 3, and 11% for the newer model versus 49, 20, and 49% for the older model, respectively.

The newer LLM extracted THA operative variables more accurately and hallucinated substantially less with simpler prompts than the 2-year-old model. These findings suggest LLMs are improving their ability to follow directions and reason without inventing information. However, lower rates of hallucinations persist, limiting trustworthiness.

Article.ArticleTitle: Modernization of a Historical Prostate Cancer Registry using Artificial Intelligence: A Tale of Two Large Language Models.

Abstract.AbstractText: Since 1986, the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry has followed over 30,000 patients who underwent radical prostatectomy. Advances in LLMs may modernize data collection, reduce human abstraction burden, and improve registry efficiency. Herein, we report the results of LLM data abstraction for surgical pathology and prostate MRI data in the Mayo Clinic Prostate Cancer Registry.

Surgical pathology and MRI reports were obtained for 3,210 and 4,739 patients, respectively, who underwent radical prostatectomy from 2010-2022. LLM prompts for 13 pathology and 20 MRI variables were developed and ran through two independent LLMs (Google Gemini Flash 1.5, 2.0, or 2.5). LLM outputs were compared to human-abstracted data.

Median consensus LLM error rate for pathology report data was 0.09%(IQR 0.03-0.16%), compared with median human error rate of 2.81%(IQR 1.83-3.17%). Individual LLMs had threefold higher error rates compared to consensus LLM (LLM 1: 0.27%(IQR 0.09-0.34%), LLM 2: 0.30%(IQR 0.17%-0.48%)). For MRI reports, median consensus LLM error rate was 0.17%(IQR 0.00-0.68%), compared with human error rate of 1.01%(IQR 0.59-3.20%). Individual LLMs had error rates of 0.84%(IQR 0.34-2.79%) and 1.02%(IQR 0.34-1.67%). Estimated time for human data abstraction across all 136,510 data elements was 952 hours, compared with 32 hours for our LLM pipeline.

LLM data abstraction employing a consensus vote across two independent LLMs consistently yielded higher accuracy than human or single-LLM abstraction. A dual-LLM consensus architecture may improve data abstraction efficiency, reduce errors, and should be considered for integration into all prospectively maintained longitudinal clinical registries.

Article.ArticleTitle: Labeling Clinical Notes With Large Language Models: Retrospective Benchmarking Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Clinical notes are rich sources of clinical information and are routinely used in clinical practice to infer past diagnoses and other comorbidities. Large language models (LLMs) may simplify the task by extracting this information from clinical notes.
The study aims to evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on the task of labeling English clinical notes.

This institutional review board-approved retrospective study comprised 380 clinical notes obtained from 2 institutions in the United States. The notes were manually labeled for the presence or absence of 29 conditions (simplified Elixhauser Comorbidity Index) by 2 human readers-a radiology resident and a medical student under the supervision of a senior radiologist. Forty-six LLMs, including 4 closed-source commercial models from the GPT and Claude families, and 42 open-weights LLMs from the Llama (13 models) and the Qwen (29 models) families were used to label each note. The GPT-o3-mini-high reasoning model was used to parse the free-text model responses to binary yes/no answers. Using the manual labels as the reference standard, the recall, precision, and F1-scores for the models were evaluated. The effect of factors such as the length of the notes and the family, size, and release recency of the LLMs was analyzed using generalized linear models.

The top-performing LLMs included the GPT and Claude models, and the larger open-weights models included Llama 3 70B, Llama 3.1 70B, Llama 3.1 405B, Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 1.5 72B, Qwen 1.5 110B, Qwen 2 72B, and Qwen 2 VL 72B, which achieved F1-scores above 70%. The most recent and higher-capacity releases of the LLMs have been improving mainly in their precision. The evaluation of 29 conditions showed a large variance in performance depending on the condition.

In this evaluation with 46 LLMs, larger open-weights LLMs such as the Llama 3.3 70B performed on par with or better than the GPT and Claude models, achieving F1-scores above 70%. The performance of open-weights models improved significantly with model size and recency. These results suggest that locally run open-weights LLMs can be potentially used to label clinical notes.

Journal.Title: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences

Article.ArticleTitle: AI-Empowered Multimodal Data Integration and Knowledge Discovery for Pharmacovigilance.

Abstract.AbstractText: Biomedical artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on heterogeneous data sources, yet differences in data structure, terminology, evidence quality, and provenance complicate their integration into reliable knowledge resources. Here, we develop an evidence-aware framework for processing and integrating heterogeneous pharmacovigilance data from FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) reports, biomedical literature, clinical trials, and electronic health records in Mass General Brigham. The framework combines large language model (LLM)-based information extraction, ontology-driven semantic normalization, cross-source evidence assessment, statistical and machine learning-based prioritization, and ingredient-based adverse drug event (ADE) relationship inference to transform heterogeneous evidence into a structured and evidence-based knowledge resource. The constructed knowledge system contains 11,588 drug nodes, 44,843 ingredient nodes, 3,275 ADE nodes, 993 indication nodes, and more than 2.47 million relationships, with each drug-ADE relationship assigned a confidence score. We further developed a drug-level web interface for accessing the knowledge resource and validated its utility in downstream AI tasks. Specifically, incorporating the developed knowledge resource improved the comprehensiveness, relevance, and overall quality of LLM-based drug-specific ADE synthesis and improved the precision and F1 score of clinical ADE relation extraction. These results demonstrate that AI-assisted processing combined with evidence-aware curation can transform heterogeneous biomedical evidence into reusable, AI-ready knowledge with explicit provenance and evidence strength information. The framework provides a general strategy for integrating heterogeneous biomedical data to support reproducible knowledge construction and downstream biomedical AI applications.

Article.ArticleTitle: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records.

Abstract.AbstractText: Large language model (LLM) agents are proposed for clinical prediction but are untested in pediatrics, where cohorts are small and outcomes are uncommon. Using records from 2,489 youth with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes (T1D), spanning structured data, note-derived social determinants and, in T1D, continuous glucose monitoring data, we predicted seven T2D outcomes, four also in T1D, at 24 months from 18 months of follow-up. CEDAR (Clinical Evidence-Driven Agent for Risk-prediction), an evidence-citing, self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine learning in both cohorts (pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.815 versus 0.656 to 0.700 in T2D and 0.756 versus 0.603 to 0.631 in T1D), most on the sparsely screened outcomes. Only 4 of 70,246 values it cited did not match the chart. Reading only the evidence and reasoning cited by CEDAR, two pediatric endocrinologists reached the same prediction as CEDAR in about nine of ten cases, agreeing with each other on 90.5%.

Article.ArticleTitle: Causal inference with real-world data in health care research: a scoping review protocol and study within a review protocol.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study will improve the understanding and application of causal inference methods in health care research using real-world data (RWD). It seeks to systematically synthesize existing methods across different data sources, and assess whether large language models (LLMs) can support key steps in review processes.

Randomized controlled trials are considered the gold standard for evaluating treatment effects, as randomization balances confounders and enables causal inference. However, randomized controlled trials are often costly, time-consuming, or ethically infeasible. As a result, RWD, such as electronic health records, medical registries, and health insurance claims, are increasingly used in medical research. Complex methods are necessary to derive causal inference from RWD.

Studies that use RWD, evaluate any type of health outcome as a primary endpoint in order to investigate patient health status, address a causal question related to a treatment or intervention, and estimate a causal effect size related to the causal question will be eligible for inclusion.

PubMed, Embase.com, and Web of Science will be searched for articles published in peer-reviewed journals between January 1, 2010, and January 29, 2026. A scoping review will be conducted to identify and categorize causal inference methods applied to RWD, focusing on theoretical frameworks, data requirements, and inferential assumptions in order to develop a taxonomy of methods. The frequency, context of use, and quality of reporting will be systematically assessed. In parallel, a study within a review (SWAR) will evaluate the performance of LLMs for title and abstract screening and full-text data extraction compared with human reviewers.

Article.ArticleTitle: American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Classification: Hybrid Machine Learning-Large Language Model Ensemble Retrospective Validation Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: The American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status (ASA-PS) classification system fundamentally shapes perioperative care delivery but suffers from poor interrater reliability (0.4-0.6). Machine learning (ML) models and large language models (LLMs) offer complementary remedies: ML processes structured data consistently but cannot interpret the nuance of clinical narratives, while LLMs parse narrative text and generate explanations but adhere inconsistently to diagnostic criteria.
This study aimed to develop and evaluate a parallel ML-LLM ensemble that combines the complementary strengths of both approaches for automated ASA-PS classification.

We retrospectively analyzed 3000 adult surgical encounters from the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences (UAMS) between August 2024 and May 2025. Cases were randomly allocated to training (n=2000), validation (N=500), and held-out test sets (N=500). The validation set was used exclusively for architecture comparison and hyperparameter tuning, and the held-out test set was reserved for final model performance validation. We developed multiple architectures, including traditional ML models (Extreme Gradient Boosting [XGBoost], Light Gradient Boosting Machine [LightGBM], ExtraTrees), an LLM-only baseline (Generative Pretrained Transformer-4o [GPT-4o]), and hybrid approaches. The parallel ensemble processed structured data through XGBoost and unstructured clinical notes through GPT-4o independently, with outputs combined via weighted averaging. Model performance was evaluated using macro-F1-score, exact match accuracy, and ±1-class accuracy.

A theoretical performance ceiling of macro-F1-score=0.59 was determined through evaluation by an expert panel of 2 board-certified anesthesiologists (AF and GF) who independently rated 50 patient charts for ASA-PS scores. On the true held-out test set (N=500), the parallel ensemble (α=0.30) achieved a macro-F1-score of 0.530 (95% CI 0.350-0.600), exact match accuracy of 0.630 (95% CI 0.580-0.670), and ±1-class accuracy of 0.980 (95% CI 0.968-0.992), exceeding the frozen LLM-only baseline evaluated on the same set (macro-F1-score 0.493, exact match accuracy 0.621,±1-class accuracy 0.981). On the validation set used for architecture selection, the ensemble outperformed structured-only ML (XGBoost macro-F1-score=0.333, P<.001), and the LLM-only model reached a macro-F1-score of 0.642 (95% CI 0.525-0.691), nominally exceeding the expert panel ceiling. Per-class analysis attributed this to a perfect score on the 2 validation ASA-PS 5 cases. Excluding that class, the adjusted macro-F1-score was approximately 0.55, within the range of the parallel ensemble. The LLM component also generated explanations detailing comorbidities, severity descriptors, and functional status indicators.

The parallel ML-LLM ensemble achieved performance approaching the theoretical ceiling established by the expert panel benchmark while providing interpretable clinical explanations. The ±1-class accuracy of 0.980 (95% CI 0.968-0.992) may enhance operational safety by minimizing extreme misclassifications. This approach demonstrates how complementary AI architectures can enhance perioperative risk assessment, which is particularly valuable given current health care workforce shortages.

Journal.Title: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association

Article.ArticleTitle: Beyond diagnostics: a scoping review of generative artificial intelligence for clinical documentation and client communication in veterinary practice.

Abstract.AbstractText: To systematically map the current landscape of generative AI (GenAI) and large language model applications for clinical documentation and client communication in veterinary medicine, critically appraise validation depth, and identify barriers to real-world adoption.

Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, CAB Abstracts, and IEEE Xplore were searched for original research published between January 2020 and June 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data using a 4-dimensional validation matrix (technical accuracy, clinical quality and safety, operational impact, and human-centric impact). Synthesis was conceptually grounded in the job demands-resources model.

10 studies met the inclusion criteria: 6 addressed clinical documentation (automated clinical coding, information extraction, and generation of subjective, objective, assessment, and plan [ie, SOAP] notes), and 4 addressed client communication (veterinary triage and automated query responses). While technical accuracy was frequently assessed, operational impact was evaluated in only 1 study, and no study employed validated psychometric instruments to measure burnout. Key barriers included clinical hallucinations, data privacy concerns, poor interoperability with practice information management systems, and absence of veterinary-specific fine-tuning.

GenAI demonstrates substantial technical promise for automating veterinary documentation and client communication tasks, yet the evidence base is characterized by a pronounced validation gap: operational and human-centric outcomes remain virtually unquantified.

Until rigorous evidence emerges, veterinarians should approach commercially available AI tools with cautious optimism. Future research must prioritize pragmatic, multicenter prospective trials employing multidimensional validation frameworks to generate evidence supporting safe clinical deployment.

Article.ArticleTitle: Evaluating RAG Configurations for Clinical Information Extraction from EHR Notes: Aged Care Case Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Clinical information extraction from unstructured electronic health records is important for supporting clinical decision making and healthcare research. However, large language models can struggle to accurately extract domain-specific information without effective adaptation. Retrieval-augmented generation offers a promising approach, but the optimal configuration for clinical information extraction remains unclear. This study evaluated different retrieval-augmented generation configurations for extracting frailty index items, malnutrition risk factors, and agitation in dementia from clinical notes collected from 40 Australian residential aged care facilities. We compared general and biomedical embedding models, LangChain and LlamaIndex retrieval frameworks, top-k values of 1, 5, 10, 15, and 20, and one to five few-shot examples using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. The best results were achieved using LangChain with the BAAI/bge-m3 embedding model, three-shot prompting, and a top-k value of five. This configuration achieved F1 scores of 97.08% for frailty index extraction, 97.14% for malnutrition risk factor extraction, and 90.52% for agitation in dementia extraction. These findings provide empirical evidence on how retrieval, embedding, and prompting choices influence clinical information extraction performance. The study offers practical guidance for researchers and healthcare informatics practitioners seeking to optimise retrieval-augmented large language model systems for extracting clinically meaningful information from unstructured aged care records.

Article.ArticleTitle: A framework for structuring Thai medical documents using systematized nomenclature of medicine clinical terms and large language models.

Abstract.AbstractText: Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine - Clinical Terms (SNOMED CT) enables semantically interoperable health data, but implementation in Thailand is hindered by language and workflow challenges. We evaluated whether large language models (LLMs) can automate SNOMED CT concept extraction from Thai clinical documents. The objectives of this study are to develop a proof-of-concept framework for automated clinical named entity recognition and SNOMED CT concept linking from Thai medical documents, and to compare the performance and resource requirements of closed-source and open-source LLMs on a human-annotated dataset. The dataset was manually annotated from 220 Thai medical documents (6,390 entities) from three outpatient departments. Our retrieval-augmented framework was evaluated using four LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4.1, Qwen 3, and MedGemma) as experimental based models which were comparatively analyzed for entity recognition using precision, recall, F1 score and concept linking using character-level metric, Intersection over Union (IoU), as well as resource consumptions. For entity recognition, Gemini achieved the highest performance (loose F1 83.31%). For SNOMED CT concept extraction ranked most similar (Top-1) by encoder models for retrieval and re-ranking, IoU scores were 39.42% (Gemini), 34.44% (GPT), 29.86% (MedGemma), and 28.62% (Qwen). Average processing time for end-to-end extraction was 5-6 minutes per document for Gemini and GPT, with cost estimates in United states dollars (USD) of USD 0.035 and USD 0.019 per document, respectively; local open-source inference required up to 10 minutes per document. This study established a proof-of-concept framework for automated clinical entity recognition and SNOMED CT concept linking from Thai medical documents, demonstrating practical LLM performance with trade-offs between accuracy, cost, and efficiency across closed-source and open-source models.

Article.ArticleTitle: Data governance framework for the implementation of automated healthcare-associated infection surveillance using large language models: Privacy-by-design with open-source de-identification pipeline.

Abstract.AbstractText: Healthcare-associated infection (HAI) surveillance remains heavily dependent on manual review of electronic medical records (EMRs), limiting scalability, reproducibility, and between-hospital comparability. Large language models (LLMs) may support extraction of clinically relevant information from unstructured text, but implementation is constrained by data protection, governance, and workflow integration challenges. Within an ECDC-funded feasibility project on healthcare-associated bloodstream infection (HA-BSI) surveillance in Italian hospitals, we developed an implementation framework to address these barriers.

The framework combines a Data Protection Impact Assessment used as a design instrument, categorization of data into raw, derived, and aggregated tiers, an on-site assisted de-identification workflow, and a tiered LLM deployment model. LLMs are used for structured clinical information extraction only, while final case classification is performed through a transparent, deterministic, rule-based algorithm based on ECDC definitions.

The project produced an operational workflow in which identifiable clinical records remain under hospital control and only locally reviewed de-identified outputs are transferred for downstream research processing. It also led to development of an open-source human-in-the-loop redaction prototype. Key implementation barriers included variable EMR maturity, document export constraints, and lengthy ethics, institutional, and data protection approval cycles. Final LLM benchmarking and surveillance-performance evaluation remain ongoing.

Trustworthy LLM-assisted surveillance may depend on governance and implementation architecture as much as on model capability. The proposed framework provides a feasibility model requiring further validation across hospitals, languages, record systems, and LLM versions.This study describes a privacy-by-design workflow for using large language models to extract clinical information from Italian hospital records while preserving local data control, enabling deterministic ECDC case-definition matching for healthcare-associated bloodstream infection surveillance through on-site de-identification and human oversight.

Article.ArticleTitle: CLINES: Clinical LLM-based Information Extraction and Structuring Agent.

Abstract.AbstractText: Clinical narratives in electronic health records (EHRs) hold diagnostic, therapeutic and temporal information often missing from structured fields; manual chart review remains the de facto standard but is slow, costly and variable. We aimed to develop and evaluate Clinical LLM‑based Information Extraction and Structuring Agent (CLINES), a pipeline that extracts and normalises clinical concepts from free-text notes into ontology-grounded, auditable, schema-ready data without task-specific fine-tuning.

We developed CLINES, a modular multistep pipeline: semantic chunking of long notes; extraction by reasoning-capable large language models (LLM); attribute assignment (assertion, value+unit); Unified Medical Language System normalisation; explicit and relative date resolution; and aggregation into an i2b2-style schema. Evaluation was conducted without task-specific supervised training on deidentified MIMIC-III, 4CE and CORAL (breast, pancreas) notes. Comparators include rule/lexicon systems, transformer encoders, single-prompt LLM baselines, alongside chain-of-thought LLMs and full-size clinical named entity recognition encoders (BERT-base, GatorTron-base). Outcomes were F1 for entity, assertion, value+unit and date processing, reported with 95% bootstrap CIs and paired-bootstrap, false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected tests. Inter-annotator agreement, hallucination taxonomy, cost and component ablations were also assessed.

Across all datasets and tasks, CLINES ranked first on every task-dataset combination. F1 ranges were 0.69-0.87 (entity), 0.84-0.93 (assertion), 0.77-0.90 (value+unit) and 0.73-0.79 (date, where gold annotations were available). Gains over the strongest single-prompt LLM were +0.21-0.38; transformer encoders trailed by +0.28-0.68 F1 on entity extraction. Performance remained stable as notes lengthened, while transformer baselines lost recall. Code field gains and most assertion/value comparisons were significant at FDR-adjusted p<0.05 on paired-bootstrap tests; mention-level inter-annotator F1 on a cross-annotated subset was 0.82 (assertion κ=0.85); a seven-class taxonomy on 700 stratified false positives found 54% of apparent false positives to be annotation gaps rather than true hallucinations.

CLINES translates narrative EHR text into ontology-grounded, auditable, schema-ready data, offering a practical route to scale chart review-like extraction for cohort discovery and real-world evidence. CLINES substantially reduces but does not eliminate the need for manual review: the residual hallucination quantified here means human verification remains necessary for safety-critical use. CLINES is model agnostic-open and closed models can be substituted to meet cost, performance and privacy goals.

Article.ArticleTitle: Evaluating a Large Language Model for Emergency Triage Using Synthetic Clinical Dialogues: Toward a Multimodal Clinical Safety Framework.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objectives: Prioritizing patient safety through accurate emergency triage is critical during mass-gathering events such as Hajj and Umrah, where high patient volumes can significantly increase the risk of clinical errors. Although the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) provides a standardized triage protocol, it remains dependent on human judgment, while traditional artificial intelligence (AI) models often struggle to capture the nuanced clinical context embedded in patient narratives. To address this gap, this study evaluates GPT-5.2 using synthetically generated dialogues as a step toward a conceptual clinical decision-support framework that bridges structured electronic health records (EHRs) with triage interactions through clinical dialogues. By combining narrative inputs with structured physiological indicators, it explores the potential to support more informed clinical decision-making under controlled simulation conditions. Methods: To evaluate this contribution, we systematically assessed the role of clinical dialogues in triage performance using a balanced and stratified dataset of 1000 simulated Hajj-context scenarios. Results: The results demonstrate that incorporating clinical dialogues can significantly improve triage performance, with a 79.7% relative reduction in under-triage across all ESI levels. A more noticeable improvement was observed in high-acuity cases, with a 91.9% relative reduction in under-triage. In addition, the model achieved a high-acuity recall of 94.5%, highlighting its ability to identify critical "red-flag" symptoms that are often not captured in structured data. These findings suggest that narrative context may contribute to more accurate triage assessment and improved identification of high-acuity cases. Conclusions: Consequently, when evaluated within a controlled decision-support setting, this study suggests that large language model (LLM)-based systems may improve triage reliability and may contribute to safer triage decision-making in high-demand clinical environments.

Article.ArticleTitle: Performance of GPT-4o in CT-based crista galli morphological classification: image-only versus morphometric dataset-driven approaches: a controlled comparative study.

Abstract.AbstractText: The aim of this study was to examine whether ChatGPT's performance in a morphological classification task based solely on a single CT slice and without access to any additional health record information varies depending on the inclusion of metric datasets.

This study is based on a CT-based classification system in which categorized the crista galli morphometrically and morphologically. Paranasal CT (PNCT) images of 101 randomly selected patients who underwent PNCT were retrieved from the hospital's database. The PNCT slices used by the radiologists for classification were uploaded individually to GPT-4o in a randomized patient order, and it was asked to perform morphological classification based solely on the CT images. The accuracy of the morphological classifications performed by GPT-4o based on the morphometric data and PNCT slices was statistically compared to the radiologists' gold standard classifications.

GPT-4o correctly classified CG types in 27.72% of cases using PNCT slices, whereas its classification accuracy reached 100% when using the morphometric dataset. The accuracy of GPT-4o's classification based on PNCT slices was significantly lower compared to its performance with morphometric data (p < 0.001). When examining the classification accuracy of GPT-4o based on PNCT slices by CG type, the highest accuracy was observed for the ossified type at 60%, while the lowest was for the tubular type at 6.06%.

Although ChatGPT has demonstrated promising performance in diagnostic radiology when provided with textual or numerical datasets, in this controlled CT-based crista galli morphologic classification task, GPT-4o demonstrated substantially lower performance when relying solely on image input compared with structured morphometric data. These findings suggest that the performance of multimodal LLMs may strongly depend on structured information. Further studies involving broader diagnostic settings are required before conclusions regarding clinical applicability can be drawn.

Article.ArticleTitle: Flexible Large Language Models for Multi-variable Extraction in Sarcoma Pathology Notes: A Pilot Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Bone and soft tissue sarcomas are heterogeneous cancers. We developed a large language model (LLM)-based extraction workflow to extract six variables from surgical pathology reports of patients with musculoskeletal sarcoma: tumor diagnosis, greatest dimension, closest margin, tumor grade, necrosis, and viability. We hypothesized that the pipeline could achieve clinically acceptable accuracy and serve as a scalable solution to augment or replace manual chart abstraction in sarcoma registry development.

We retrospectively collected 1106 surgical pathology notes of patients who underwent surgical resection of bone or soft tissue sarcoma at three sites of a single institution. Notes were split into a training set (n = 353) and a testing set (n = 753). Prompt engineering and fine-tuning were used to query the open-source LLMs Llama3-70B-Instruct and Gemma4-31B-Instruct. Accuracy, F1 score, and specificity were calculated to evaluate the performance of extracted points.

On the testing set, both models achieved accuracy of at least 0.85 on extracting all data points and specificity of at least 0.84 on predicting "unknown" when data were not available in the note. The Gemma model achieved higher sensitivity on detecting positive margins than the Llama model: 0.92 versus 0.78. Both LLMs took less than 1 second on average to extract each data point from each pathology note.

Registry development for heterogeneous cancers such as sarcoma is limited by the labor-intensive nature of manual data abstraction, and our pipelines achieved promising results. These findings support the feasibility of LLM-based workflows as scalable and accurate alternatives to manual data abstraction for sarcoma clinical registries.

Article.ArticleTitle: Generative Large Language Models for Psychiatric Concept Detection in Spanish-Language Electronic Health Records: Development and Evaluation Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: The accurate detection of clinical symptoms in electronic health records (EHRs) is pivotal for advancing large-scale genetic and longitudinal studies in psychiatry. Free-text clinical notes are an essential source of symptom-level information, particularly in psychiatry; however, the automated extraction of symptoms from clinical text remains challenging.

We aimed to evaluate the ability of open-source generative large language models (LLMs) to detect psychiatric symptom-level concepts from clinical text in Spanish and to develop a new fine-tuned, open-source LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information.

We tested 11 open-source generative LLMs for their ability to detect 109 psychiatric concepts from clinical text, using annotated EHR notes from a psychiatric hospital in Colombia. The LLMs were evaluated both "out-of-the-box" and after fine-tuning and compared against a traditional natural language processing (tNLP) method developed from the same data. To develop a fine-tuned LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information, we created a novel synthetic dataset, leveraging real concept annotations while generating fully synthetic clinical text, and fine-tuned a top-performing LLM on these data. Fine-tuned model generalizability was assessed through cross-site evaluation using data from a second independent hospital in Colombia.

We show that while base LLM performance was poor to moderate (zero-shot: 0.2-0.6 macro-F1; few-shot: 0.2-0.74 macro-F1), it improved significantly after fine-tuning (0.75-0.86 macro-F1), with several fine-tuned LLMs outperforming the tNLP method. In total, 100 psychiatric concepts could be reliably detected (F1>0.8) using either a fine-tuned LLM or tNLP. Using the synthetic dataset, we developed Mistral-small-psych, a new LLM capable of detecting psychiatric concepts from Spanish clinical text with performance comparable to models trained on real EHR data (macro-F1=0.79) while remaining fully distributable. In cross-site evaluations, most LLMs generalized well, with small out-of-domain performance losses (macro-F1 decrease of 0.02-0.16).

This work provides the first large-scale, cross-institutional evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs for psychiatric concept detection in Spanish EHRs, introduces a privacy-preserving pathway for building shareable clinical natural language processing models, and presents a new open model for extracting symptom-level psychiatric information from Spanish clinical text.

Article.ArticleTitle: Transformer models in cardiovascular medicine: current applications, translational challenges, and future directions.

Abstract.AbstractText: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide, highlighting the need for improved early detection, accurate diagnosis, and personalized therapeutic strategies. With advances in artificial intelligence (AI), Transformer-based models have attracted increasing interest because they can model long-range dependencies, support large-scale pre-training, and integrate heterogeneous data. Originally developed for natural language processing, Transformers have been extended to medical image analysis, physiological signal interpretation, and clinical text mining. In cardiovascular medicine, these models have been applied to electrocardiogram interpretation, cardiac imaging, electronic health record analysis, multimodal data integration, digital-twin development, and large language model-enabled workflows. Although many studies report promising performance, clinical value remains contingent on data quality, external validation, calibration, workflow integration, and trustworthy governance. This narrative review provides a focused overview of Transformer-based models in cardiovascular medicine, critically evaluates their translational limitations, and outlines priorities for clinically useful and responsible cardiovascular AI.

Article.ArticleTitle: From chatbot to clinical copilot: the role of generative artificial intelligence in nuclear medicine reporting and data extraction.

Abstract.AbstractText: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming clinical documentation workflow. This scoping review evaluates the emerging role of LLMs in nuclear medicine and molecular imaging, as recent literature suggests increasing evaluation of newer LLM architectures alongside GPT-4. We conducted a scoping review following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Lens, and Google Scholar was performed from January 2023 to January 2026. Studies were included if they applied LLMs to nuclear medicine tasks (PET/computed tomography, single-photon emission computed tomography, and scintigraphy). General radiology studies were only included if separate nuclear medicine data were extractable. A total of 14 studies were included. While the GPT-4 family remains the most studied, recent literature includes increasing evaluation of non-GPT models, with several studies reporting comparable performance in specific tasks. In data extraction tasks, such as tumor-node-metastasis staging for breast cancer, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and DeepSeek have demonstrated performance comparable or superior to GPT-4o. The applications are primarily categorized into generative reporting (drafting impressions) and data extraction (structuring unstructured text). However, limitations persist: LLMs struggle with dynamic curve analysis (e.g. renal scintigraphy) and visual interpretation. Safety remains a concern, with one study reporting an 8% rate of potentially harmful responses in patient education scenarios. LLMs are evolving from experimental chatbots into capable 'Clinical copilots' that can significantly reduce administrative burden through automated reporting and data structuring. However, because of risks of hallucinations and domain-specific limitations in dynamic imaging, human oversight remains non-negotiable. Future research must focus on multimodal integration and multicenter prospective validation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Zero-Shot Extraction of Structured Clinical Data from Free-Text CT Reports Using Foundational Large Language Models.

Abstract.AbstractText: Large language models (LLMs) are being explored for multiple applications in medical research, including medical text classification. Authors of the study evaluated the performance of three off-the-shelf LLMs in classifying unstructured free-text CT pulmonary angiography reports for pulmonary embolism (PE)-related diagnostic labels.

Authors assessed human-labeled CT reports using three LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, Llama 3.3 70B, and Llama 3.1 8B) with zero-shot simple and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts. Classification tasks included acute PE (N = 1,025) and, among reports with PE (n = 660), bilateral PE and large PE.

LLMs demonstrated high classification performance for acute PE and bilateral PE but lower performance for large PE. With simple prompts, the highest F1 scores were 97.0% for acute PE (Llama 3.1 8B; sensitivity, 95.6%; specificity, 97.3%), 92.9% for bilateral PE (ChatGPT-4o; sensitivity, 98.0%; specificity, 88.6%), and 72.8% for large PE (ChatGPT-4o; sensitivity, 82.9%; specificity, 82.2%). CoT prompting did not meaningfully improve acute PE classification but provided slight improvements in subclassification performance for bilateral and large PE.

Off-the-shelf LLMs can classify free-text CT reports using simple prompt engineering and may facilitate automated data extraction for medical research following appropriate evaluation of classification performance.

Article.ArticleTitle: Development of a large language model clinical variable extraction pipeline for the study of lymphedema.

Abstract.AbstractText: For many disease processes, clinical information is often captured in unstructured clinical notes that require manual data extraction for research. Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to automate the data extraction process, enabling study for diseases with fewer tabular metrics available. Here, we report the development and validation of an LLM-based clinical note data extraction approach for a retrospective cohort study of lymphedema etiologies and treatments. After using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision codes to identify potential lymphedema patients and text-matching to find potentially relevant clinical notes, an LLM was used to further filter notes, summarize for relevant content, and extract per-patient variables concerning etiology, treatments and efficacies, clinical stage, and wound status. Prompts were optimized for accuracy with an iterative review strategy, starting with zero-shot approaches and modified to few-shot approaches where necessary, validated by subset human review. A Protected Health Information-compliant Application Programming Interface version of OpenAI's GPT-5 was used for all LLM queries. Human review of LLM-extracted final variables revealed high accuracy when compared against both an intermediate summarization step (99% accurate) and against original clinical notes (98% accurate) across 2858 patients/32,288 notes. LLMs are a valuable tool for conducting clinical research at scale using unstructured text data.

Article.ArticleTitle: Reducing Annotation Costs Using Knowledge Distillation for Label‑Efficient Negation Detection in Radiology Reports: Multisite Internal Validation Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Negation in radiology reports (eg, "no evidence of dissection") is essential for accurately conveying diagnostic information. Clinical natural language processing systems, however, often fail to determine whether findings occur within negated or speculative contexts, leading to excessive false keyword alerts, noise in information extraction, and reduced precision in downstream clinical or research applications. Transformer models have advanced detection capabilities but require costly expert labeling. Large language models (LLMs) may provide label-efficient alternatives through few-shot prompting or knowledge distillation.

This study aims to systematically evaluate LLMs and transformer models under different supervision strategies, including comparisons of expert-labeled and LLM-distilled transformers, teacher LLMs (GPT-5.3 Chat, Gemma 4, and Qwen3.6-Plus), sampling approaches, and direct few-shot LLM inference, to determine whether LLM inference or LLM-based distillation can substitute for human labeling in radiology-report negation detection while reducing annotation costs.

We reused and analyzed 6000 deidentified English-language radiology reports from 3 hospital branches. Three LLMs-GPT-5.3 Chat, Gemma 4, and Qwen3.6-Plus-performed 0-, 5-, and 10-shot inference to identify negations and speculations unrelated to abnormal findings and generate pseudo-labels for transformer fine-tuning (Bio_ClinicalBERT [Bio + Clinical BERT model], BERT [Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers], and ALBERT [A Lite Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers]). We trained models using human-labeled or LLM-distilled supervision across 28 training data scales (n=42-4200) and 3 data sampling seeds and compared them across multiple supervision and training conditions encompassing backbone, label source, and sampling strategy. We assessed performance using keyword-level precision, recall, and F1-score with paired bootstrap tests (10,000 replicates).

We refined 1000 report annotations (interrater κ=0.957) and fine-tuned 1260 transformer models. Human-labeled transformers consistently outperformed distillation-labeled ones, with the largest gap at small training scales (ΔF1-score ≈0.042; adjusted P<.001), which narrowed at larger scales (ΔF1-score ≈0.022; adjusted P<.001). Teacher model choice had minimal effect on distilled performance. All 3 human-labeled transformer backbones (BERT, ALBERT, and Bio_ClinicalBERT) achieved high keyword-level F1-scores (0.982-0.985 under their best conditions; n=4200). In the 10-shot setting, GPT-5.3 Chat (F1-score 0.974) modestly underperformed human-labeled transformers in the large-sample range (ΔF1-score=0.009; adjusted P=.047) and significantly outperformed Gemma 4 (F1-score 0.957; adjusted P=.01) and Qwen3.6-Plus (F1-score 0.950; adjusted P<.001) in the bootstrap analysis. GPT-5.3 Chat labeled reports at approximately US $0.018 per report and became less expensive than manual annotation when expert hourly wages exceeded US $0.64-1.50.

Human-supervised transformers remain the strongest baseline, but frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.3 Chat offer comparable performance with minimal supervision. LLM-based distillation offers a cost-effective alternative with only minor performance loss. Dataset scale proved more influential than sampling strategy. Additionally, superior teacher performance yielded no proportional gains through distillation, as open-weight or low-cost teachers achieved comparable results. If supported by external validation, the proposed label-efficient framework could enable accurate and affordable negation detection and rapid domain adaptation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Synthetic Medical Document Generation Pipeline (MedDocSynth) for Optical Character Recognition: Development and Validation Study on Korean Clinical Documents.

Abstract.AbstractText: The development of structured optical character recognition (OCR) systems for Korean medical documents is hindered by strict privacy regulations that limit access to real clinical data. Existing synthetic document frameworks are primarily designed for generic layouts and Western languages, and fail to capture the complex formatting, bilingual terminology, and hierarchical field semantics required for clinical OCR and document-understanding tasks in hospital environments.

This study aimed to develop and validate a privacy-preserving, template-driven pipeline for generating realistic synthetic Korean medical documents with structured XML annotations, enabling OCR and document-understanding model training in settings where access to real clinical data is restricted.

We designed MedDocSynth, a 7-stage synthetic document generation pipeline that reconstructs authentic medical document layouts from publicly available references, incorporates clinician-guided template selection, and uses a structured placeholder system encoding 17 medical data types. Human-curated templates were populated with exemplar content and tagged using a delimiter-based scheme, after which GPT-4o-mini generated diverse synthetic values for each field. The pipeline produced 1000 fully synthetic DOCX documents with corresponding XML annotations encoding hierarchical structure, title-answer relationships, and datatype metadata. We evaluated text fidelity, lexical diversity (type-token ratio, measure of textual lexical diversity [MTLD], n-grams, and Pareto), and compared the system with existing synthetic document pipelines. A Qwen2.5-VL model was fine-tuned exclusively on the synthetic dataset and evaluated on 50 real-world Korean clinical documents to assess OCR accuracy, information extraction, and table reconstruction.

The pipeline achieved 100% placeholder coverage, 99.68% format correctness, and 91.56% semantic accuracy. Lexical diversity analysis demonstrated high variability in free-text fields (MTLD≈456) and expected repetitiveness in structured datatypes. Compared with existing pipelines (SynthText, SynthTiger, and DocSynth), the proposed system uniquely supports complex clinical forms, bilingual content, and structured XML annotations. When trained solely on the synthetic data, Qwen2.5-VL achieved the highest real-world performance, with a character accuracy of 86.01%, word accuracy of 78.25%, field accuracy of 67.18%, datatype accuracy of 64.14%, and table reconstruction tree-edit-distance similarity score of 71.09%. Models without fine-tuning performed substantially worse, including GPT-5-mini.

We present the first synthetic data generation pipeline specifically tailored to Korean medical documents, enabling the creation of realistic, richly annotated datasets for structured OCR without exposing patient information. The synthetic data significantly improves OCR performance on real clinical documents, demonstrating the pipeline's potential utility for hospital deployment and its potential extensibility to other languages and health care systems.

Journal.Title: Journal of the Korean Society of Radiology

Article.ArticleTitle: Large Language Models in the Radiology Workflow: Current Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives.

Abstract.AbstractText: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted increasing research interest in radiology owing to their capacity for natural language processing and, more recently, multimodal image-text reasoning. This review provides a clinically oriented overview of LLM applications across the radiology workflow, encompassing scan protocols, image interpretation, radiology reporting, and communication with patients and clinicians. Although the existing general-purpose multimodal LLMs show promise in diagnostic tasks, their image-interpretation performance is limited; they often prioritize textual context over visual information, and they are prone to hallucinations. In contrast, LLMs have demonstrated practical utility in radiology reporting, including structured radiology reporting, summarization, automated data extraction, and clinically meaningful report categorization. This review also discusses the reporting guidelines and performance evaluation methodologies specific to LLM research to promote more scientifically rigorous and reproducible studies in this rapidly evolving field. Finally, we outline the future directions for LLM research to support the responsible and effective integration of LLMs in radiology practice.

OtherAbstract.AbstractText: 대형 언어 모델(large language models)은 자연어 처리 능력과 최근의 멀티모달(multimodal) 이미지-텍스트 추론 능력을 바탕으로 영상의학 분야에서 각광을 받고 있다. 본 종설은 영상의학 워크플로우 전반에 걸친 대형 언어 모델의 활용을 임상 중심으로 개괄하며, 검사 프로토콜 결정(scan protocoling), 영상 해석(image interpretation), 판독문 작성(radiology reporting), 그리고 환자 및 임상의와의 의사소통(communication)을 포함한다. 현재 멀티모달 대형 언어 모델은 진단 작업에서 가능성을 보이고 있으나, 영상 해석에서는 신뢰성이 아직까지는 제한적이며 시각 정보보다 텍스트 맥락을 우선적으로 활용하고 환각(hallucination)이 발생하기 쉬운 경향을 보인다. 반면, 판독문 작성 분야에서는 구조화된 판독문 생성(structured radiology reporting), 요약(summarization), 자동 데이터 추출(data extraction), 그리고 판독문 분류(categorization)와 같은 영역에서 실질적인 유용성을 입증하였다. 또한 본 종설에서는 빠르게 발전하고 있는 이 분야에서 보다 과학적으로 엄밀하고 재현 가능한 연구를 촉진하기 위하여, 대형 언어 모델 연구에 특화된 보고 지침(reporting guidelines)과 성능 평가 방법을 논의한다. 마지막으로, 영상의학 임상에서 대형 언어 모델을 책임감 있고 효과적으로 적용하기 위한 향후 발전 방향을 제시한다.

Article.ArticleTitle: Relationship extraction for adverse drug events in clinical notes using large language models: a retrospective cross-sectional study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Adverse drug events (ADEs) are a critical indicator of patient safety but are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. The potential of recent advances in natural language processing (NLP), particularly generative large language models (LLMs), to identify ADEs remains understudied. This study aimed to compare the performance of multiple LLMs in identifying ADE-Drug relationships in inpatient and ambulatory clinical notes.

We used clinical notes from the 2018 National NLP Clinical Challenge (n2c2) ADE dataset (inpatient; n = 505) and from outpatient encounters (n = 2555) between October 1, 2018, and December 31, 2019, at a large academic medical center based in New England. Notes were pre-processed into snippets for model input. Evaluated Models included: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.2-3B and their instruction fine-tuned variants (including low-rank adapters for Llama). Performance was assessed using both strict and relaxed evaluations (precision, recall, and F1) for all models, followed by manual evaluation (exact semantic match, partial match, missing ADE, drug mention only, not a drug, or wrong) of the two best-performing models.

Of the 1048 notes in the local test split, 450 (42.9%) contained at least one ADE. The n2c2 test set included 202 notes, of which 155 (76.7%) contained at least one ADE. GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini were the top-performing models among those evaluated. GPT-4o consistently outperformed GPT-4o-mini in ADE extraction across both datasets, with higher F1-scores (0.524 vs. 0.381) and a more balanced precision-recall profile. Both models captured ADEs effectively in explicit and complex clinical contexts, although limitations included misclassification of pre-existing allergies and occasional conflation of therapeutic indications with adverse effects. GPT-4o achieved higher exact match coverage and fewer errors across clinical notes, indicating more reliable performance in both inpatient and ambulatory settings.
This work establishes a foundation for integrating LLM methods into real-world drug safety surveillance, with direct implications for improving patient safety.

Article.ArticleTitle: Optimizing Clinical Temporal Relation Extraction With Large Language Models: Comparative Analysis.

Abstract.AbstractText: Clinical temporal relation extraction (CTRE) is essential for reconstructing patient timelines from unstructured electronic health records (EHRs). However, the linguistic complexity of clinical notes and the high cost of expert annotation impede the development of large-scale training corpora. While large language models (LLMs) have transformed general natural language processing, their application to CTRE remains underexplored.

This study aimed to determine the optimal adaptation strategy for CTRE by conducting a controlled comparative benchmarking of LLM architectures and fine-tuning methodologies in both data-rich and limited-data regimes.

We evaluated 4 LLMs representing 2 distinct architectures-transformer encoders (GatorTron [University of Florida and NVIDIA]) and transformer decoders (LLaMA 3.1-8B [Meta AI] and MeLLaMA-13B [Yale University and University of Florida]). We compared four adaptation strategies: (1) standard fine-tuning, (2) hard-prompting, (3) soft-prompting, and (4) low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Experiments were conducted on the 2012 i2b2 CTRE benchmark in both full-supervision and 1-shot scenarios.

Recent LLMs combined with appropriate adaptation strategies achieved strong performance for CTRE on the 2012 i2b2 benchmark. In the data-rich setting, the best-performing configuration was LLaMA3.1-8B with quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) applied to the query and value projection layers, achieving a micro-F1-score of 89.15% (0.30). Comparative analyses showed that QLoRA applied only to the query and value projection layers achieved performance comparable to QLoRA applied to all linear layers, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Hard-prompting showed particular effectiveness in the 1-shot scenario compared with standard fine-tuning for GatorTron-Base. Overall, Decoder-based models generally outperformed encoder-based models under QLoRA-based adaptation. However, under the most resource-constrained setting, where both training data and trainable parameters were highly limited, encoder-based models achieved better performance than decoder-based models.

This study provides a controlled benchmark for adapting LLMs to CTRE under different data and parameter constraints. Our findings suggest that QLoRA targeting only the query and value projection layers is a computationally efficient and competitive adaptation strategy. Decoder-based LLMs generally achieved stronger performance under QLoRA-based adaptation, whereas domain-specific encoder-based models showed advantages under the most resource-constrained soft-prompting setting. These results highlight the importance of selecting adaptation strategies according to both model architecture and available computational resources.

Article.ArticleTitle: Advances in Multimodal Artificial Intelligence in Radiology: Data Integration, Foundation Models, and Clinical Applications-A Narrative Review.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background/Objectives: Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in radiology to combine medical images with radiology reports, clinical narratives, structured health records, laboratory measurements, and other patient data. These systems may support more context-aware interpretation, reporting, and clinical decision-making than unimodal approaches. This narrative review examines recent technical and clinical advances in multimodal radiology AI and identifies barriers to responsible implementation. Methods: Relevant biomedical and technical literature was identified through targeted searches of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, Scopus, arXiv, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar. A documented screening process identified 111 reviewed publications from 1154 records. Study selection and data extraction were conducted by one reviewer without independent verification. Original research, reviews, and commentaries, including selected preprints, were synthesized thematically. Results: The field has progressed from early and late feature fusion toward cross-modal attention, contrastive image-text pretraining, vision-language models, multimodal large language models, and general-purpose foundation models. Applications include diagnostic classification, prognostic modelling, image-text retrieval, visual question answering, clinical decision support, and automated radiology report generation. Despite promising technical results, comparison across studies remains difficult because of heterogeneous datasets, tasks, metrics, and validation designs. Clinical translation is further limited by scarce external and prospective validation, uncertain interpretability, hallucination and omission risks, privacy and fairness concerns, and limited real-world workflow evaluation. Conclusions: Multimodal AI may enable more clinically informed radiological interpretation and reporting, but progress in benchmark performance has outpaced evidence of safety, generalizability, and clinical utility. Future research should prioritize multicentre evaluation, clinically meaningful metrics, transparent reporting, robust safety assessment, and workflow-centred implementation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Applications of transformer-based pretrained language models for analyzing nursing records in adult care: A scoping review.

Abstract.AbstractText: Nursing records contain clinically meaningful information but remain underutilized due to their unstructured narrative format. Transformer-based pretrained language models, including encoder-based pretrained language models (PLMs) and decoder-based generative large language models (LLMs), are increasingly being used to analyze these records, yet the landscape of their applications remains unclear.

To map the application of these models to nursing records in adult care, including the records analyzed, analytical tasks and clinical purposes, methodological approaches, model performance, and reported limitations.

This scoping review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Scopus were searched from inception through May 2026 for studies applying these models to unstructured nursing records in adult care. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and assessed full texts. Data were extracted by one reviewer and independently verified by two reviewers. Findings were synthesized descriptively.

Thirty-two studies published between 2021 and 2026 were included. Encoder-based PLMs (n = 19) were adapted mainly by supervised fine-tuning, whereas decoder-based generative LLMs (n = 13) were used mainly through prompting. Both architectures were applied primarily to classification and information extraction, most often to identify patient conditions or predict clinical outcomes. Summarization was conducted in two studies. Model performance was not comparable across studies because of heterogeneous evaluation conditions and limited reporting of uncertainty. Only one study reported prospective silent evaluation; none evaluated clinical deployment or effects on clinical outcomes. Generalizability was the most frequently reported limitation (n = 14).

Transformer-based pretrained language models have been applied to nursing records mainly to transform narrative text into predefined categories, with little use of approaches that leverage the narrative characteristics of these records. Validation has largely remained confined to model development settings, limiting conclusions about clinical applicability. Future research should prioritize external and prospective validation and investigate tasks and adaptation strategies suited to nursing records.

Article.ArticleTitle: Dataset of anonymized clinical events and notes from obstetric electronic health records for NLP.

Abstract.AbstractText: Interoperability remains a global challenge in healthcare systems. Addressing the need for standardized health data to ensure compatibility would enable large-scale clinical data analysis and systematic studies across heterogeneous databases, generating statistical information to support the analysis of health conditions. Healthcare data documented in Spanish face a critical limitation: the limited availability of standardized, representative, and publicly accessible real-world clinical datasets to support the development and evaluation of data-driven approaches, including Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications for treatment support, diagnosis, patient monitoring, and observational research. Analyses conducted on proprietary hospital data models are often subject to population-specific biases. Moreover, artificial intelligence applications, such as NLP using large language models (LLMs), face significant constraints due to heterogeneous clinical workflows and non-standardized storage schemas. Adherence to standardized data models, supported by syntactic and semantic standardization processes, facilitates multicenter and large-scale observational research. In this work, we present a Spanish-language dataset comprising 23,879 electronic health records (EHRs), each corresponding to a unique patient treated in a gynecology and obstetrics setting at the Clínica Universitaria Bolivariana, a national reference institution in Colombia. The dataset was standardized according to the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (version 5.4). It includes both structured and unstructured patient data from deliveries attended between 2015 and 2017. The dataset contains >3.7 million anonymized clinical notes in Spanish natural language, preserving confidentiality and privacy. It integrates 89,893 clinical events from which 200,070 observations related to diagnoses and procedures are derived, together with associated clinical documentation. Standardization under the OMOP framework enables harmonization with additional data sources to address research questions and to generate clinical evidence for large-scale observational studies. This dataset supports reuse in research focused on the development, training, and evaluation of tools-particularly in clinical NLP in Spanish-as well as comparative studies between structured data and free-text clinical documentation in large-scale healthcare settings, thereby contributing evidence grounded in real-world medical practice.

Article.ArticleTitle: A non-destructive methodological framework for modernizing legacy clinical reporting systems for AI-driven pharmacoinformatics: a SAS case study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Legacy clinical reporting pipelines bottleneck drug development and pharmacovigilance: they encode regulatory-grade analytical logic but produce opaque output with no machine-readable intermediate layer, resisting integration with artificial intelligence (AI). Existing modernization approaches force a choice between full rewrites that abandon validated logic and incremental refactoring that preserves structural barriers to AI access. We present a non-destructive framework that achieves AI-driven pharmacoinformatics readiness without altering legacy source code. A metadata layer - a bridge map, a typed Intermediate Representation (IR), and an orchestrator - wraps existing reporting components, re-exposes their outputs as structured data consumable by large language models (LLMs), and enables optional incremental consolidation of selected components while the remainder operates unchanged. On a 558-component industrial SAS reporting library (373,000 lines of code), the framework demonstrated immediate AI readiness under coexistence mode with the legacy library unchanged. Where consolidation was elected, the modernized core achieved a 92% reduction in consolidated-core SAS lines of code (excluding the Python and YAML layers). Parity validation on 14 report types from an internal Phase III study cleared an 80% cell-level triage-admission gate on 11 of 14 reports (mean across all 14 report types 82.7%, best 99.2%); the three remaining reports differed in table-layout geometry rather than in computed values. A public benchmark on CDISC CDISCPilot01 data achieved 100% regression-consistency against frozen reference outputs across 5 reports (4,764 cells, 0 mismatches) - a reproducibility benchmark rather than independent validation. In a proof-of-concept study with a single large language model, the IR illustrated the feasibility of table summarization, adverse-event anomaly detection (a pharmacovigilance signal-detection example), and trial configuration generation - feasibility rather than validated performance. The framework offers a regulation-aware path to AI-integrated clinical trial reporting intended to reduce modernization overhead without interrupting ongoing regulatory submissions. Its regulatory-traceability features are design properties rather than validated compliance: no formal Installation/Operational/Performance Qualification (IQ/OQ/PQ) has been performed. All results derive from a single case study; the methodology is designed to be reusable across organizations and library scales, pending multi-site empirical validation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Reproducible synthetic clinical letters for seizure frequency information extraction.

Abstract.AbstractText: Seizure-frequency information is critical for epilepsy research and clinical decision-making, yet it is often documented in highly variable free-text neurology clinic letters that are difficult to share and annotate at scale. This study focused on adult epilepsy clinic letters from patients aged 18 years or older. We aimed to develop a reproducible and privacy-preserving framework for seizure-frequency information extraction by training models using fully synthetic, task-faithful clinical letters.

We designed a structured label scheme that captures common linguistic patterns of seizure burden, including explicit rates, numeric ranges, cluster-based descriptions, seizure-free durations, unknown frequency, and explicit no-seizure statements. A high-capacity teacher language model was used to generate NHS-style synthetic epilepsy follow-up letters paired with normalised labels, step-by-step rationales, and evidence spans. We fine-tuned multiple open-weight large language models (4-14B parameters) to extract seizure frequency from full letters using either direct numeric outputs or structured labels, optionally augmented with evidence-grounded explanations. Performance was evaluated on a clinician double-checked held-out set of real clinic letters using both fine-grained and pragmatic frequency groupings.

Models trained purely on synthetic letters generalised to real-world letters, and structured label targets consistently outperformed direct numeric regression. With 15,000 synthetic training letters, representative models achieved micro-F1 up to 0.79 (fine-grained) and 0.85 (pragmatic) on the real test set, while a medically oriented 4B model reached 0.79 and 0.86, respectively. Evidence-grounded outputs supported rapid clinical verification and facilitated error analysis.

Task-specific synthetic clinical letters with structured, evidence-grounded supervision enabled reproducible development of seizure-frequency extractors while reducing reliance on sensitive adult patient text. These findings support this approach for adult epilepsy clinic-letter extraction, but do not establish generalisability to paediatric notes or other clinical domains.

Article.ArticleTitle: Extracting smoking history from clinical notes for lung cancer screening decision support: comparing a structured-judgment model with general-purpose large language models.

Abstract.AbstractText: To compare the accuracy, cost, and speed of a low-cost, non-generative structured-judgment model and four general-purpose large language models (LLMs) for extracting smoking status, pack-years, and quit date from clinical notes to support lung cancer screening (LCS) clinical decision support (CDS).

We built a synthetic, shareable benchmark of 3,000 outpatient notes in three conditions: 1,000 template-generated notes, 1,000 realistic, ``messy'' notes written by an LLM from structured facts, and 1,000 ``messy'' notes that required complex arithmetic to determine pack-years and quit dates. Ground truth reference labels were programmatically generated before each note was created. We compared TypeSafe Jev 1.13 with Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6 Sol, each using an identical structured output schema. We determined United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) 2021 and American Cancer Society (ACS) 2023 eligibility from each system's output in code.

Jev made the correct eligibility decision for 99.1%, 99.9%, and 94.4% of notes in the three conditions, compared with 97.8%, 98.4%, and 98.1% for Haiku, 100.0%, 99.6%, and 99.8% for Sonnet, 99.7%, 98.8%, and 98.5% for Luna, and 100.0%, 99.8%, and 99.6% for Sol. In the complex condition, Jev produced 27 false positive and 14 false negative screening flags per 1,000 notes, the most of any system. Luna cost $0.12 to $0.21 per 1,000 notes and Jev $0.61 to $0.64, compared with $2.44 to $4.22 for Sol, $3.37 to $4.43 for Haiku, and $3.76 to $6.61 for Sonnet. Jev was the fastest system (median 0.45 to 1.21 seconds per note, compared with 1.71 to 3.50 seconds for the others).

All models tested had high accuracy. The structured-judgment model had the lowest latency, which could allow for synchronous use in clinical decision support systems rather than batched, cached invocation. The cost of the structured-judgment model was low, but the newest cost-efficient LLM, Luna, was less expensive and more accurate on the complex notes, though its latency was higher. Accuracy, latency, and cost are all moving quickly as new models are released.

Fast, low-cost language models could make real-time, note-based CDS practical, and current models are highly accurate. Prices and capabilities are changing rapidly, so continuous benchmarking and system updates are essential.

Article.ArticleTitle: Leveraging Large Language Models for Temporal PHI De-identification in Real-World Clinical Notes.

Abstract.AbstractText: De-identifying temporal protected health information (PHI) is challenging because temporal expressions appear in diverse formats and must be transformed while preserving clinically meaningful timelines. This study proposes and evaluates an LLM-based framework for temporal PHI de-identification in real-world clinical notes. Using 1,148 notes from 30 sarcoma patients (28,431 annotated temporal entities), we evaluated multiple modern LLMs for temporal entity extraction and surrogate generation. Proprietary models achieved strong extraction performance, with GPT-4o achieving the best overall results. Most models preserved temporal formatting (>99%), but surrogate generation remained challenging. GPT-5.4 achieved the highest shift correctness (90.2% on a shared-entity subset) and the lowest order violations. Error analysis revealed systematic shift deviations (±1, ±30/31, ±365 days), highlighting persistent limitations in LLM temporal reasoning. These findings suggest that reliable temporal de-identification will require hybrid or multi-agent approaches beyond standalone LLMs.

Article.ArticleTitle: Leveraging Generative Large Language Models for Temporal Relation Extraction From French Clinical Narratives: Prompt-Chaining Approach.

Abstract.AbstractText: Temporal relation extraction (TRE) in clinical narratives is crucial for understanding patient history, disease progression, and treatment pathways. However, it remains challenging due to limited annotated data and to the complexity of clinical text, including domain-specific terminology, inconsistent information, and implicit temporal reasoning. These challenges are particularly acute for rare diseases, where information such as the date of diagnosis or the onset of key phenotypes is rarely available in structured data, despite being essential for estimating diagnostic delay and reconstructing the natural history of the disease.

We explore the potential of open-weight and on-premises large language models (LLMs) on clinical TRE and normalization using zero- and few-shot prompting, aiming to reduce the time-consuming and costly annotation process. Based on recent promising capabilities of LLMs in understanding and reasoning over text, we evaluate whether these models can efficiently perform TRE and normalization in real-world clinical settings.

We cast the temporal relation task as a question-answering task, in which the models extract the temporal expressions associated with a given clinical event. We propose a prompt-chaining strategy that sequentially performs normalization on the extracted temporal expressions. Our LLM-based approach is evaluated on constructed and annotated French real-world clinical narratives, covering temporal relations involving 2 types of clinical events: phenotypes and rare disease diagnoses. Four open-weight LLMs were evaluated across multiple prompt configurations and compared with rule-based and neural baselines using exact-match metrics, an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and human validation. We further evaluate our approach by applying it to the English 2012 i2b2 corpus, involving other types of clinical events.

The proposed approach achieves stable extraction performance with only a small number of in-context examples across both clinical event types, reaching a maximum F1-score of 0.72 for rare disease diagnoses and 0.61 for phenotype events. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation supports these findings by capturing minor temporal variations penalized by exact-match metrics, while human validation further confirms the clinical validity of the extracted relations. On the 2012 i2b2 corpus, the approach remains robust despite increased complexity and minimal supervision. Adding normalization using the prompt-chaining strategy maintains stable overall performance, indicating minimal error propagation and efficient temporal normalization.

Prompting LLMs with a minimal set of in-context examples can achieve strong performance for TRE and normalization in low-resource settings with limited domain-specific annotations. Relying on open-weight, on-premises models, the proposed approach therefore offers a practical path toward deployment in real-world clinical workflows and could further be extended to extract key clinical information, such as age at diagnosis or age at onset, particularly in the context of rare diseases, where it could help prefill structured reporting forms, reducing the manual effort needed to retrieve such information directly from clinical narratives.
